study.title: Psalm 79 - I am sorry for devastation and hope of restoration
study.overview: This psalm is a community lamentation that describes the ruin of Jerusalem, the profanation of the temple, the violence against the people and the public shame caused by the nations. The voice of the psalmist does not deny the sin of the people, but asks that divine wrath not remain upon Israel forever. At the same time, he appeals to the name of God: that his honor be defended, that forgiveness come, that the oppressed be saved and that the people return to praise him from generation to generation.

outline.title: The holy city profane and the humiliated people
outline.explanation: The first verses describe the invasion of the nations, the contamination of the temple, the destruction of Jerusalem, and the exposition of the dead bodies without burial. The regret goes to shame before the neighbors and shows that the crisis has reached both the worship and public dignity of the people.

outline.title: The cry for mercy, forgiveness and help
outline.explanation: The psalmist asks even when the wrath of God will last, but also asks that this anger lies upon the enemies that do not know the Lord. Then the request changes to repentance and supplication: that God does not remember the old guilt, but come with mercy, help, forgiveness and deliverance for the sake of his name.

outline.title: Visible Justice and Continuous Praise of Praise
outline.explanation: The second half asks the nations to see God's response to the shed blood and the groaning of prisoners. The psalm ends with a future confidence: the people of God, like the sheep of their pasture, will praise them forever in all generations.

study.context: The notes link this psalm more likely to destroy Jerusalem and the temple, associated with Babylonian exile. The setting includes the ruined city, the desecrated temple and the people in deep distress. The notes also note that this lament talks closely with the tone of Jeremiah, and that verses 6 and 7 are taken back in Jeremiah 10:25. The historical context is therefore that of a national catastrophe that resulted in both public humiliation and penitent prayer.
study.theology: The psalm unites three central theological truths. First, God remains the Lord of history: the nations act, but they do not escape from the divine government. Second, God's discipline does not cancel his mercy; the people recognize their guilt and ask for forgiveness, showing that restoration is not born of merit, but of divine compassion. Third, the honor of God's name is an essential part of the petition: deliverance is asked that the nations do not falsely conclude that the God of Israel has been defeated. There is also a right tension between repentance and justice: the people confess weakness and sin, but ask God to treat violent enemies responsibly. In the Protestant evangelical reading, this points to the hope that God forgives, restores, and makes his people a testimony of lasting praise.

scholarViews.insight: The psalm is understood as a lament linked to the fall of Jerusalem and the desolation of Zion; the psalmist asks forgiveness and ransom, and also that God repays the enemies of the nation.
The petition of verse 6 is seen as very appropriate to the affliction of the church: it is asked that the wrath of God deviate from his people and falls upon those who persecuted and abuse them.
The final verse expresses the identity of the chosen people and of the sheep of God's pasture, with the promise of perpetual gratitude in all generations.

questions: What changes in prayer when the people move from simple pain to the request for forgiveness and restoration?
How does the psalm show that public shame and material ruin also belong to the spiritual life of God's people?
How today can we seek deliverance without forgetting that the honor of God's name is central?
study.practice: Practical reading: When life or church appear in ruins, this psalm teaches how to bring pain to God honestly, without makeup of sin or despair of mercy. A concrete application is to turn crises into specific prayer: confessing one's own frailty, asking for forgiveness when necessary, praying for help and making the desire for restoration an opportunity to witness the name of God faithfully. It is also a call not to romanticize injustice: the text allows to cry out for justice in the face of violence, but always before the Lord and not as personal revenge.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided do not allow the human author to be safely determined, the exact date of the composition or all the details of the historical situation; the link with the Babylonian exile is the most likely reading, not an absolutely demonstrable fact only by the text. There is also a difference in emphasis between the commentators on the framework of the psalm, although everyone agrees to relate it to the ruin of Jerusalem and the supplication by restoration.
